title: Xing Mobility introduces immersion-cooled batteries for ships - electrive.com
content:
Xing Mobility is launching two immersion-cooled battery systems specifically for maritime applications. The modular Immersio XM25 solution is adaptable to different ship types, while the Immersio CTP, with its cell-to-pack architecture, is designed to offer particularly high energy density in a compact space.
Image: Xing Mobility
Xing Mobility will present two battery systems for maritime applications at SMM 2026, an international maritime trade fair taking place in Hamburg, Germany, from 1 to 4 September. The manufacturer describes the Immersio XM25 and Immersio CTP as next-generation battery systems developed specifically for marine environments. As the company states: “Both systems are based on our patented immersion cooling technology, in which every single battery cell is fully surrounded by an electrically non-conductive cooling fluid.”
Xing Mobility is, at its core, a Taiwanese developer of immersion cooling technology for batteries. In immersion or submersion cooling, the battery cells are completely flooded with coolant. Typically, cooling plates or channels only touch one or two sides of a battery cell, meaning heat transfer occurs over a significantly smaller surface area than with immersion cooling. This technology is designed to dissipate heat efficiently and prevent thermal runaway in individual cells, as well as the spread of fire throughout the entire pack.
In July 2022
, Xing Mobility introduced the Immersio XM25, initially targeting heavy-duty commercial vehicles.
In August 2023
, the company followed with its first cell-to-pack battery solution, the Immersio CTP, which is also suitable for electric cars. At the
Paris Motor Show in autumn 2024
, the Taiwanese company presented a cell-to-chassis solution. Most recently, at
IAA Mobility 2025
, Xing Mobility introduced a CTP battery specifically designed for sports cars.
Against this backdrop, Xing Mobility describes the Immersio series as a flexible battery pack concept that can be adapted to the “specific requirements of various vehicle types, such as saloons, SUVs, sports cars, commercial vehicles, and more.” The company manufactures the packs at its production facility in Taiwan, which opened in 2024.
Xing Mobility has now adapted the latest batteries in the Immersio family for ships and will present them at SMM 2026. However, the company has provided only broad details about their properties and no performance data. The modular design of the XM25 allows it to accommodate different vessel types, while the CTP system uses a cell-to-pack architecture that “achieves double the energy density of conventional marine batteries” and supports continuous 3C discharge. Xing Mobility designed both systems to deliver consistently high performance, improve fire safety and reduce onboard space requirements.

title: Sila awarded $1.4bn loan for US silicon anode and Li cells expansion – Batteries International
content: US silicon carbon anode developer Sila Nanotechnologies has secured a conditional $1.4 billion federal loan to support an expansion of manufacturing at its facility in Washington state. Sila confirmed the agreement with the Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital on August 7, saying the deal will also help expand lithium ion battery cell manufacturing at the firm’s Moss Lake site. The funding aims to help Sila develop its Titan Silicon anode technology and establish a silicon battery cell facility for speciality applications with what the firm said are rigorous performance requirements — such as industrial, agricultural, and military drones. The loan was announced during a mining investment event attended by President Donald Trump — where he announced more than $2 billion in critical mining and mining-related projects to revitalise the industry, including over $180 million in mining school investments to bolster the American mining workforce. Federal backing for Sila comes against a backdrop of what the US government said are significant technology sovereignty challenges, with a structural deficit in domestically produced battery materials and high-performance battery cells. China controls over 90% of anode material processing and over 80% of global battery cell production, leaving American manufacturers of critical defence technology exposed to a single point of failure, Sila said. Co-founder and CEO Gene Berdichevsky said: “We solved the hardest problem in battery materials with the invention of the modern silicon anode. But invention is only the first step — manufacturing it at gigascale here in America proves that technology sovereignty is possible.” The financial boost follows a $300 million equity round in July 2026 led by Sutter Hill Ventures and Atreides Management. Also in July, lead battery industry leaders in the US welcomed new controls aimed at controlling exports of recoverable critical battery minerals including lead, tin and antimony. Battery Council International said a directive issued by the US president addressed longstanding concerns of the battery recycling industry and would support the domestic battery supply chain and national security. title: Samsung SDI buys GM out of Indiana battery project to focus on EVs, BESS – Batteries International
content: Samsung SDI is ending its existing battery cells joint venture project with General Motors in Indiana — and acquiring the US auto giant’s stake in the plant under construction in New Carlisle. However, the South Korean battery firm said on August 11 it had signed a new agreement with GM to jointly develop a next-generation prismatic battery cell for potential future EV applications. The move allows Samsung to establish its first independently operated battery production base in North America, which will now have an initial focus on producing ESS batteries. The new deal comes just two months after Samsung and GM announced their $3.5 billion Indiana partnership was on “pause”. Samsung has now agreed to acquire GM’s 49.99% stake in the SynergyCells joint venture set up by the two. Samsung said the arrangement was made in consideration of market changes since the joint venture was announced — including slower-than-expected growth of EV demand. Construction of the battery plant is already underway. The facility will initially be used to produce ESS batteries with the potential to include prismatic cells jointly developed with GM. A Samsung spokesperson said: “While reflecting recent market changes, this acquisition decision is to continue the strategic partnership with GM. We will continue our commitment to an electrified future with the partner, while utilising the plant to proactively respond to the fast-growing ESS market in the US.” When the joint venture project was announced in 2024, the partners said they would invest around $3.5 billion to build the plant, which would have an annual production capacity of 27GWh initially, targeting mass production in 2027. These home batteries pair solar storage with whole-home backup; the newest models combine the inverter, controls, and even EV charging into a single cabinet.
August 11, 2026

Until renewables entered the mainstream, most residential homes were entirely dependent on the electric grid for all their power. Utilities generated power at central plants, pushed it down the lines, and homeowners paid for whatever the meter recorded. If a homeowner wanted backup power during a storm, they needed a gas generator that would always be loud and fuel-hungry.
Rooftop solar changed the game because it could theoretically generate enough power on its own to meaningfully reduce or eliminate a home’s dependency on the grid. However, households still needed to deal with solar’s intermittency: solar panels generate most of their energy during the day, but homes use most of their energy at night.
That’s why home battery storage started gaining traction. These on-site energy storage solutions decouple solar energy generation and usage, making homes with solar panels much more grid-independent. Now, as the surrounding technology, supply chains, and ecosystem have matured, home battery storage is becoming a standard option for a residential solar installation.
Related:
Understanding Base Power’s role in energy storage solutions
Today, the residential battery storage market is advancing quickly. Manufacturers are bundling the inverter, the battery, and the energy-management brain into single click-together units, extending warranties to 15 years, and building systems in the United States to meet the domestic-content rules attached to the federal storage tax credit. Whole-home backup that switches over in milliseconds, once a premium upgrade, is becoming the baseline expectation. A few of the newest systems even bring electric-vehicle charging into the same enclosure.
Picking among them comes down to how a home already makes and uses power, how much backup a family wants, and which ecosystem a local installer supports. We've put together a list of seven residential battery storage systems worth buying this year. Read on to learn what sets each one apart.

Jaguar offers first look at the Type 01 EV interior
The Type 01 is “unmistakable from every angle,” according to Rawdon Glover, Jaguar’s managing director, and “the interior is no different.”
Jaguar previewed the interior for the first time as it prepares to reveal the electric GT in full in October.
Like the exterior design, the inside is the first to debut Jag’s new “creative philosophy,” which stirred up the social media folks when it was first unveiled.
After Jaguar revealed the radical GT concept in late 2024, everyone from Tesla CEO Elon Musk to Lucid Motors chimed in,

and the brand’s desperate attempt to reinvent its image.
Inside, the Jaguar Type 01 features a minimalist four-seat layout with a “dramatic” central spine to create four individual spaces.
As a stark contrast to the Jags we’re accustomed to, a large display sits in front of the driver, while a small touchscreen is added where you would typically find cupholders. Speaking of which, it doesn’t appear to have any.
A digital ClearSight Rear View Display is featured at the base of the windshield to help the driver focus.
Rather than the typical wood finish, the Type 01 has a brass-inspired finish on the central spine, doors, and part of the steering wheel. The steering wheel and door panels include physical buttons.
“With a confidence‑inspiring GT driving position, clean and sophisticated technology and dramatic styling, Type 01 has an interior like no other,” Glover said. Do you agree?

title: This $1,800 electric motorcycle hits 70 MPH and could change the game
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Aug 12 2026 - 8:05 am PT
A new player in the industry,
, thinks its EX2S electric motorcycle could shake things up with impressive performance and accessible pricing.
The Indian company is competing in a crowded market with several electric competitors, not to mention the litany of gasoline-powered motorcycles already crowding the showrooms. But with these figures, it may stand a chance.
India is already the world’s largest two-wheeler market, selling more than 20 million motorcycles and scooters each year. Now this new electric motorcycle from startup Avore is showing just how quickly that market is evolving – and at a price that could make riders elsewhere more than a little jealous.
The new Avore EX2S is priced at just ₹169,999, or an equivalent of around US$1,800. For that money, which significantly undercuts other electrics like the
Royal Enfield Flying Flea C6,
buyers get a commuter-focused electric motorcycle with performance figures that are surprisingly impressive.
The bike packs a 5 kWh battery offering a
161 miles (260 km) of range on India’s IDC testing cycle. That’s a completely unreasonable range rating, landing at nearly the efficiency of an electric bicycle (31 wh/mi or 19 wh/km), but we’ve seen before how optimistic the official IDC numbers can be. Real-world range is likely to be closer to half that figure, but even 80 miles (130 km) would be plenty for most urban applications.
Power comes from a 10.5 kW (14 hp) permanent magnet synchronous motor capable of producing a claimed 250 Nm (184 lb-ft) of wheel torque. That helps the EX2S sprint from 0-25 mph (40 km/h) in just 2.8 seconds before continuing on to a top speed of 70 mph (114 km/h). But again, anyone who wants to enjoy the top end of that speed range will be in for a good time – not a long time.
Charging is another highlight. An onboard 1.5 kW charger plugs directly into a standard household outlet, taking the battery from 20% to 80% in around two hours or fully charging it in roughly four hours. Avore also says its split-pack battery architecture improves weight distribution and thermal management compared to a single large battery pack.
Despite the bargain price, the EX2S doesn’t skimp on technology. A 7-inch TFT display offers navigation and ride data, while smartphone connectivity enables geo-fencing, diagnostics, and security alerts. Riders can also choose between multiple riding modes, including a simulated four-speed “SYFT Mode” that mimics traditional motorcycle gear shifts.
The EX2S is currently aimed squarely at the Indian market, and there’s no indication Avore plans to export it anytime soon. That’s a shame, because while riders in the US likely won’t be buying one soon, it’s another reminder that some of the most exciting developments in affordable electric motorcycles are happening far outside North America.

title: Ford has a new $25,000 crossover SUV coming, but will it go electric?
content:
The crossover SUV will be Ford’s lowest-priced vehicle, starting at around $25,000. According to dealers who were shown a preview of the vehicle, it will not be based on the Universal EV platform.
Is Ford launching a $25,000 EV crossover SUV?
After announcing the name and starting price of its new midsize electric pickup last week, the Fathom, Ford is apparently working on an even more affordable vehicle.
Ford offered dealers a glimpse of its upcoming lineup last week during a private meeting in Las Vegas, including a new crossover SUV set to arrive in 2029.
According to an Automotive News report, attendees said the entry-level model was a boxy, wide SUV. One said it resembled the first-generation Escape.
Ford did not reveal many details outside of previewing early mock-ups in a video, but the crossover is expected to start at around $25,000. That would make it the brand’s lowest-priced vehicle positioned below the current Maverick.
Surprisingly, the new SUV will not ride on Ford’s Universal EV platform, like the Fathom pickup. Instead, it will reportedly be offered as a hybrid and a gas-powered vehicle.
The new crossover SUV is expected to go into production in 2029 at Ford’s Hermosillo Assembly Plant in Mexico.
In the meantime, Ford will open pre-orders for the all-electric Fathom pickup in early 2027, starting at $28,350.
Ford said the EV pickup will compete “in the heart of the affordable EV market,” starting at under $30,000. Deliveries are set to begin later in 2027.
Electrek’s Take
After investing so much time and resources in developing the new Universal EV platform, why not release an all-electric SUV on it?
Top comment by BarelyLucid
“After investing so much time and resources in developing the new Universal EV platform, why not release an all-electric SUV on it?”
The answer is pretty straightforward. Those resources were invested in a factory in Louisville, not the factory in Mexico where this SUV will be produced. An ICE SUV from an ICE factory in 2029 doesn’t mean they won’t also have an EV SUV from an EV factory on a similar timeframe. A lot rides on the Fathom being both a production and market success, which would push ford to continue/accelerate plans to covert plants to the new EV platform production process.
Ford has said the UEV platform is flexible enough to support vehicles ranging from B-car-sized vehicles to commercial vans, so we could still see an affordable electric crossover at some point. When and if remains up in the air.
In the first half of 2026, four out of the top five best-selling EVs in the US were relatively affordable SUVs, including the Chevy Equinox EV, Toyota bZ, Hyundai IONIQ 5, and Tesla Model Y. The Tesla Model 3 ranked second.
Ford’s Mustang Mach-E ranked seventh, but sales dropped 46% from the first half of 2025 to just 11,632 units.
Should Ford replace the aging Mach-E with an electric entry-level crossover SUV? It seems like a no-brainer. Share your thoughts in the comments below.

title: Waymo has nearly 1,000 robotaxis waiting at its Arizona factory
content:
Waymo has 684 of its new Ojai robotaxis finished and ready to deploy at its factory in Mesa, Arizona, according to the latest aerial count of the site.
That’s out of 953 Ojai vehicles on the lot in total, or 72% already converted. It’s the clearest sign yet of how much driverless capacity Waymo is stockpiling.
A monthly count from the sky
Every month, a watcher on the r/waymo subreddit, jjricks_, posts an annotated aerial photo of the Waymo Magna factory in Mesa and tallies the robotaxis sitting on the lot. The August update counts 953 Ojai units: 684 finished, meaning fully retrofitted with sensors and ready to ship, and 269 still new and waiting for conversion.
There’s a new detail this month too. The count found 12 finished Hyundai IONIQ 5 robotaxis on the lot, the first time Waymo’s second purpose-built vehicle has shown up finished at the factory.
This isn’t official Waymo data. But the monthly series has been a consistent window into the ramp, and the trend is steep: the same tracker counted roughly 500 Ojai units back in early June.
What the Ojai is, and why Magna matters
The Ojai is Waymo’s first purpose-built robotaxi. The base vehicle is built in China by Zeekr, shipped to Mesa, and retrofitted by supplier Magna with Waymo’s sixth-generation Driver system.
That sixth-gen hardware is the whole point. It runs 13 cameras and four lidars, 42% fewer sensors than the previous generation, and Waymo has said the suite costs under $20,000 per vehicle. Cheaper sensors on a cheaper base vehicle is how Waymo builds a fleet it can actually afford to scale.
And scaling it is.
The Ojai is replacing the aging Jaguar I-Pace fleet, which was never designed for the job and costs far more to run. Waymo started offering paid rides in the Ojai in San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Phoenix earlier this year.
Why ~700 finished robotaxis is a big deal
Waymo is already doing about 500,000 paid rides a week across roughly a dozen cities, and it’s targeting one million weekly rides before the end of the year. The company operated in the low thousands of vehicles earlier in 2026.
Against that base, a reserve of 684 finished robotaxis sitting ready to go is huge. If Waymo puts even a chunk of them on the road quickly, it’s one of the biggest single additions to its fleet ever.
And this isn’t a pile of unfinished cars stuck in a queue. At 72% converted, the retrofit line is keeping pace with the Zeekr deliveries. Production isn’t the bottleneck, and neither is the conversion. The only question left is how fast Waymo turns finished inventory into paying rides.
The 12 IONIQ 5s point at what’s next. Waymo is adding a second vehicle to the same factory, which is how you scale past one supplier.
Electrek’s Take
This is a lot more exciting than watching Tesla try to deploy Cybercabs, and the reason is simple.
Top comment by Beario
It is good to see Waymo adding to their fleet. The robotaxi industry is still currently really small so in a few years the market should scale significantly in size. Each company has advantages and disadvantages. Waymo has the fast start, but they do not control their own means of production and instead rely on suppliers for vehicles. Tesla has the advantage in producing their own cars, but lack a working system that is not yet fully autonomous like Waymo. It will be interesting to see how things work for both Tesla and Waymo in the coming years though and there is bound to be a lot more competition for robotaxi's as well.
Waymo has already solved the hard part. It runs a real, fully driverless service at scale, no human in the car, half a million paid rides a week and climbing toward a million. That’s a solved Level 4 problem being scaled up. So when close to 700 finished robotaxis show up ready at one factory, it maps directly onto more rides, more cities, more revenue. The tech works. This is just adding units to it.
Tesla is not there. Its unsupervised “Robotaxi” service is still a couple dozen Model Ys in Austin after more than a year, and it’s still proving it can run without a safety monitor at all. One factory lot with 684 finished Waymos on it holds more driverless capacity than Tesla has put on public roads, period.
So the number to watch now is deployment, not production. Waymo clearly knows how to build and convert these things fast. If it can push finished cars into service at the same pace, the one-million-rides-a-week goal stops looking aspirational and starts looking conservative. And there’s a second vehicle already stacking up behind the Ojai. How fast can they flip the switch?

title: Gas prices are about to go even higher. Here’s how to use an e-bike to save money
content:
oil and gas
Micah Toll
| Aug 12 2026 - 5:33 am PT
If you are like most people and currently drive a gasoline-powered car, the pain is about to become even worse. US government officials
have warned
that gas prices are expected to rise further as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz continue to disrupt the global oil supply.
While we can’t control geopolitical events, we can control how much gasoline we actually need to buy. And that’s where e-bikes come in.
Sure, an electric car could cut down your gas bill, but that requires spending tens of thousands of dollars – not exactly an enticing proposal when you’re trying to save money.
But electric bikes may be the answer. They’re more than just those things the neighborhood kids cruise around on in packs, popping wheelies. E-bikes are also a major part of the changing US transportation landscape – and a growing part, at that. Plenty of people have discovered they
can save serious money
And it may be easier than you think. A lot of people are under the mistaken impression that switching to an e-bike means giving up their car entirely. It doesn’t.
Instead, think of an e-bike as a tool that chips away at your gas bill one trip at a time.
For most Americans, the majority of daily trips are single-passenger trips and are surprisingly short. Running to the grocery store, grabbing coffee, commuting a few miles to work, heading to the gym, picking up takeout, or visiting friends are all trips that can often be done on an e-bike instead of in a two-ton vehicle that burns gasoline just to move one person.
The beauty is that you don’t need an expensive e-bike to make this work. There are
plenty of solid options
around the $1,000 mark.
Whenever someone asks me for a good, inexpensive recommendation and isn’t sure exactly what they want, I generally start by recommending bikes like the Lectric XP4.
At just $999
, it offers enough range and capability to replace a surprising number of car trips without breaking the bank. It’s also fairly fast, up to 28 mph (45 km/h), and has surprisingly good components for its price. When you’re saving on fuel, parking, maintenance, and wear on your car, that investment can pay for itself much faster than many people realize.
Even just considering fuel, a tank of gas often costs around $50-75 in the US right now, which can add up to serious savings quickly for each trip you perform on an e-bike. But all those other car-related costs tip the scales even more heavily in the favor of e-bikes, and help them pay for themselves even faster.
Another tip is to stop thinking about replacing miles and instead focus on replacing errands. It’s easy to look at a 20 mile (32 km) commute and decide an e-bike won’t work. But maybe your grocery store is only two miles away. Maybe the pharmacy is three miles away. Maybe your favorite restaurant is a quick 10 minute ride. Those are easy wins that don’t require changing your entire lifestyle.
If carrying cargo is your concern, don’t let that stop you. Modern e-bikes can be equipped with rear racks, panniers, baskets, trailers, and even child seats. I’ve hauled groceries, camera gear, home improvement supplies, and enough Costco purchases to surprise more than a few skeptical drivers.
I can’t remember the number of times I’ve carried lumber on the back of an e-bike, but it’s definitely more than I can count on my fingers.
Finally, don’t forget that you can mix transportation methods. Ride your e-bike to work a couple of days each week instead of five. Use it on weekends. Take it whenever the weather cooperates.
Every mile you ride is one less mile your car has to. And that’s more gas money you’ve saved, not to mention the wear and tear, maintenance, parking fees, etc.
So no, an e-bike isn’t the answer to every transportation need. But it doesn’t have to be. The goal is less about extremes and more about reducing how often you’re forced to buy increasingly expensive gasoline.
And with fuel prices looking like they may be headed in the wrong direction for the foreseeable future, there’s never been a better time to start replacing car trips with bike rides.
It costs me around 15 cents to “fill up”. Can a dollar take you 200 miles? On an e-bike, it easily can!

title: France sees sharp rise in solar module recycling - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
France collected 13,760 tonnes of end-of-life solar modules in 2025, up 40% from the previous year, as recycling activity accelerates.
Government agency Soren expects annual volumes to reach nearly 180,000 tonnes by 2040, underscoring the growing importance of recycling to Europe’s industrial supply chain.
Gwénaëlle Deboutte
12 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
The Soren and Envie2E recycling plant in Saint-Loubès in Gironde | Image: Soren
Soren, the French state-approved organization responsible for managing end-of-life photovoltaic panels, says it has “reached a milestone” in its 2025 activity report. The year saw unprecedented growth in the French photovoltaic recycling sector, with 13,760 tonnes of panels collected, a 40% increase compared with 2024.
“These figures reflect the reality of a sector that is becoming more professional, organized, and mature,” said Nicolas Defrenne, CEO of the organization, which was established in 2015.
Working with recycling partners Envie 2E, Galloo, Rosi, RVE, and First Solar, Soren oversaw the processing of more than 12,736 tonnes of panels in 2025, achieving a recovery rate of more than 90%. Of this total, 10,684 tonnes were recycled, 1,298 tonnes underwent energy recovery, and 754 tonnes were sent for disposal.
180,000 tonnes of panels annually by 2040
Glass, aluminum, copper, and mineral fractions are among the materials returned to the circular economy through recycling. “At a time when demand for silver, silicon, or copper could increase four- to sixfold by 2040, photovoltaic panel recycling is no longer a niche issue; it is a strategic imperative for European industrial sovereignty,” Defrenne said.
“The volume of end-of-life panels will grow exponentially in the coming years, and we must prepare for this today,” the organization said. By 2040, nearly 180,000 tonnes of photovoltaic panels are expected to reach the end of their useful life annually in France.
In 2025, Soren had 600 member producers, whose eco-contributions generated just over €12 million ($13.8 million). The organization’s budget stood at €15.47 million, supplemented by revenue from the sale of recycled materials (€2.33 million) and financial income (€0.79 million).
Operational costs represented the largest expenditure category, at €7.35 million, including €2.69 million for collection and €4.66 million for processing. They were followed by allocations to provisions for future liabilities, which amounted to €5.41 million.
At the end of 2025, cash and provisions for future liabilities totaled €35.49 million.

title: Europe's largest battery comes online in Scotland - pv magazine Global

Coalburn 1 is the first of three UK transmission-connected battery energy storage system (BESS) projects developed by Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) to enter commercial operations.
Matthew Lynas
12 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Energy storage for Coalburn 1 was supplied by Canadian Solar’s e-Storage division. | Image: Canadian Solar
The 500 MW/1 GWh Coalburn 1 BESS has entered commercial operations at a former coal mining site in Scotland, according to CIP. The project is now the largest operational BESS in Europe.
Construction at the Coalburn 1 site in South Lanarkshire, near Glasgow, began in November 2023 according to CIP’s local development partner Alcemi. CIP divested 50% of the project to insurer Axa IM Alts in April 2025.
Revenues for Coalburn 1 will include a 10-year optimization agreement with SSE, plus a 15-year capacity market contract covering 300 MW of power output, plus a seven-year contract covering 75 MW. The project will be managed by independent renewables company RES, which signed an
agreement in July 2025
to manage the site.
Coalburn 1 is the first in a trio of 1 GWh BESS projects CIP is developing in Scotland. Coalburn 2 and
are also being built as transmission-connected assets.
Battery technology provider e-STORAGE
, a subsidiary of Canadian Solar, is supplying all three projects. The fund divested a stake in Devilla in June, sharing risk with outside funds.
Nischal Agarwal, partner at CIP, said the successful delivery of Coalburn 1 was an important milestone for the renewables investor.
“As Europe’s largest operational battery energy storage system, Coalburn 1 will enhance the flexibility and resilience of the UK electricity system, support the integration of more renewable power, and contribute to lowering costs for consumers. Alongside Coalburn 2 and Devilla this project demonstrates CIP’s industrial capabilities in developing, commercializing and delivering energy infrastructure at scale.”
CIP is working on a portfolio of battery storage facilities in the United Kingdom with local partner Alcemi. Including Coalburn 1, the portfolio consists of seven grid-scale BESS projects with a combined power output of 4.3 GW.

title: Korea’s Shinsung E&G opens 350 MW PV module production line - pv magazine Global

Patrick Jowett
12 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Manufacturing
South Korea
Image: Shinsung E&G
Korean industrial engineering and green energy company Shinsung E&G has launched a new solar module production line in South Korea.
The Gimje plant, located in the southwestern province of Jeollabuk-do, is intended to serve as a core production base for the broader Saemangeum development area.
A spokesperson for the company told
pv magazine
the modules produced by the production line use n-type cell technology. The new line has a production capacity of 350 MW, the spokesperson added, while the Gimje factory’s total capacity stands at 600 MW.
“We currently have no plans for further expansion, but if domestic market demand grows in the future, we plan to respond by bringing the remaining line into operation,” the company said.
Shinsung’s CEO, Lee Ji-sun, adds that the facility is the company’s only solar module manufacturing base in the Jeollabuk-do region and will establish the area as a “genuine hub for high-power module production.”
The production line is set to supply high-power modules to a number of project contracts Shinsung has secured in the region, including an 80 MW ground-mounted project, another 74 MW project and a 300 MW floating solar project in the
Saemangeum development area
Shinsung established the Gimje plant under an investment agreement with the city and says it has since worked on local job creation and industrial development in the area.
Shinsung’s spokesperson also told
pv magazine
the company is operating two additional factories alongside its new Gimje plant.
“The Yongin factory, in Gyeonggi-do, uses renewable energy and an energy storage system to meet its power needs. It produces cleanroom products including fan filter units and can produce up to 650 a day at maximum capacity,” the spokesperson explained. “Meanwhile, our Jeungpyeong factory in Chungcheongbuk-do produces air conditioning equipment.”
Last November, a
47.2 MW floating PV project
, featuring modules provided by Shinshung E&G, was switched on in South Korea. At the time, the project was billed as the country’s largest floating solar array located alongside a multi-purpose dam.

title: Weidmüller unveils new PV connectors - pv magazine Global

Weidmüller has introduced a tool-free PV-Stick connection system designed to simplify and speed up photovoltaic installations while ensuring reliable connections up to 1,500 V DC.
Ralph Diermann
12 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Utility-scale
The PV-Stick can operate at temperatures ranging from minus 40 C to plus 85 C. | Image: Weidmüller
Weidmüller, a German manufacturer of electrical engineering products, has developed a new connection technology designed to make photovoltaic installations simpler, faster and safer. Its tool-free “Snap-In” technology reportedly enables quick and reliable cable connections without the need for crimping tools.
The connection engages immediately, providing both electrical and mechanical integrity. According to the manufacturer, installers can connect cables in a matter of seconds. This can reduce installation time while also minimizing the risk of faulty assemblies.
The system is designed for voltages of up to 1,500 V DC and is certified by TÜV Rheinland in accordance with IEC 62852. The PV-Stick can operate at temperatures ranging from -40 C to 85 C. Its IP65 and IP68 protection ratings are designed to ensure reliable operation in outdoor conditions.
The connection technology is compatible with standard solar cables in accordance with IEC 62930:2017, allowing the product to be integrated into a range of system designs without requiring specialized cabling.

title: Unlimited long duration, long-lived pumped hydro storage - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Solar- and wind-dominated grids need abundant long-duration storage, and off-river pumped hydro offers enormous potential, with 800,000 sites worldwide and storage capacity vastly exceeding global requirements. Pumped hydro is mature, low-cost, long-lived, and locally deployable, complementing batteries by providing economical deep storage for periods of low wind and solar generation.
International Solar Energy Society (ISES)
12 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
The upper reservoir of the Tianhuangping Pumped Storage Power Station in Anji, Zhejiang, China | Image: Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0
We need a plenty of long-duration rechargeable storage in solar- and wind- dominated electricity grids for night-time, and to ride through cloudy and windless days and weeks. Fortunately, there is unlimited off-river
pumped hydro
: 800,000 sites around the world with 86 million GWh of combined storage which is enough to absorb nearly 3 years of global electricity production.
Pumped hydro is highly mature, with more than 100 years of operating experience, and widely deployed, with over 200 GW of capacity. It has low water use because water is recycled in a closed loop, requires no mining, uses less land than equivalent batteries, and has high local content, unlike batteries, which are largely imported. No new dams on rivers are required. Its capital cost per kWh is substantially lower than that of equivalent batteries, and its lifespan is much longer, at up to 150 years.
Globally abundant pumped hydro sites
We may take
50 kWh (0.05 MWh) per person
as a rule-of-thumb requirement for rechargeable storage for an affluent person relying on solar and wind for all energy. This is equivalent to an EV battery per person. For perspective, Australia (which generates the most solar electricity per person) will soon have 18 kWh per person of rechargeable pumped hydro and battery storage.
Global regions have 70 times to 500 times more pumped hydro storage potential than required.
The top 21 jurisdictions by population host 80% of the global population. Only Bangladesh has insufficient pumped hydro sites. Nigeria and India have 16 times and 22 times more sites than required, respectively. Most countries have more than 100 times the sites required, providing an abundant choice of potential sites.
A detailed spreadsheet is here
Pumped hydro
Global Pumped Hydro Atlas
, sites are listed in the size range 5 GWh to 5000 GWh, and ranked by indicative capital cost as AAA, AA, A, B, C, D and E. Roughly speaking, 5000 GWh provides sufficient rechargeable storage for 100 million affluent and fully decarbonized people who derive all their energy from solar and wind.
For perspective, 5 GWh would be a very large utility battery, while Snowy 2.0 under construction in Australia has storage of 350 GWh at a cost of US$30-40 per kWh and with a lifetime of 150 years. Mountainous countries have many sites with indicative costs half that of Snowy 2.0. Pumped hydro is cheap ($/kWh) because the marginal cost of doubling energy storage is merely the cost of scooping more rock from the bed of the reservoirs to make the dam walls higher.
Pumped hydro and batteries together solve energy storage. Batteries provide high-power intra-day storage and mobility solutions in the size range of kilowatt-hours, megawatt-hours and gigawatt-hours. However, batteries are over-powered for deep storage, and that unnecessary power is expensive. A 100-hour 1 GW battery costs about the same as a 2-hour 50 GW battery (both 100 GWh). The lifetime of Li-ion battery is one tenth that of pumped hydro (150 years).

title: New online map shows Germany's renewable energy feed-in capacity across distribution grids - pv magazine Global
content: New online map shows renewable energy feed-in capacity across German distribution grids Fifty-three photovoltaic systems with a combined capacity of 638 kW feed into the distribution grid operated by Max Peissker in Kaulsdorf, Thuringia, while 575,136 PV systems with a combined capacity of around 13.5 GW feed into the Bayernwerk Netz grid. The figures come from a new, freely accessible online map published by the evu+ initiative, part of the Edna Federal Association for Energy Market & Communication. Updated every six months, the map shows the number and capacity of generation plants and storage systems connected to the distribution grids of Germany’s 871 grid operators. Battery storage systems are also included. Users can analyze the data by grid operator, federal state, generation technology and other criteria. The map does not, however, show available grid capacity. Martin Käßler, who works in communications and marketing at edna member Fraunhofer IOSB-AST in Ilmenau, created the map with AI assistance, using data from the Core Energy Market Data Register (Marktstammdatenregister). In July, the Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur) published a map showing supply quality across Germany’s distribution grids. It uses different colors to indicate how quickly and comprehensively grid operators are implementing the energy transition and the extent to which they are using digital solutions. “The frequently voiced criticism that Germany has too many grid operators misses the mark,” said Richard Plum, managing director of the edna Federal Association for Energy Market & Communication. “Our new map impressively demonstrates that small and medium-sized grid operators, in particular, make an indispensable contribution to electricity supply and security of supply.” According to Plum, these operators are also key drivers of the energy transition, as electricity generation within their grids relies almost entirely on renewable energy sources. The association rejects criticism that Germany’s distribution grid landscape is too fragmented. It points to other European countries for comparison. Denmark has around 55 distribution grid operators and Finland 75, giving both countries a grid operator density relative to population size similar to Germany’s. Germany has around 98,000 inhabitants per distribution grid operator. By comparison, Austria has around 75,000 inhabitants per operator, with 120 distribution grid operators in total, while Switzerland has around 15,000 inhabitants per operator and approximately 600 operators. The Edna Bundesverband Energiemarkt & Kommunikation e.V. focuses on market communication processes, digitalization and IT standardization in the energy sector. Its members include municipal utilities, grid operators and energy suppliers, as well as software manufacturers and IT service providers serving the energy industry. title: South Korea approves upper limits on renewable energy setback distances - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
South Korea’s government has approved new national limits on the setback distances that local governments can impose on renewable energy installations in a bid to open up more suitable sites for future solar and wind projects.
Patrick Jowett
12 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
South Korea
Utility-scale
Image: Daniel Bernard/Unsplash
The government of South Korea has amended rules governing renewable energy facilities to introduce a new national limit on the setback distance local governments can impose on new projects.
Under changes to the enforcement decree on renewable energy projects, approved by the cabinet this week, local governments will be permitted to establish setback requirements for solar projects of no more than 200 meters, equivalent to around five houses.
The new setback distance does not apply to
community-participatory power generation facilities
, solar systems mounted on buildings, or PV systems installed for self-consumption.
The amendment also introduces a setback distance of 1,500 meters for future wind energy projects and stipulates that wind turbines must be located at least twice their total height from relevant areas.
These newly-approved setback distances, due to come into effect in September, are set as upper limits, meaning local governments retain the ability to establish their own setback distances lower than the threshold.
An update posted by the country’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (MCEE) explains that a municipality currently requiring solar projects to be at least 300 meters from residential areas would have to reduce its maximum setback to 200 meters or less, while a municipality with a 100 meter setback would be able to retain its existing rule.
MCEE’s statement adds that setback requirements have historically varied significantly across South Korea’s local governments. A total 129 of the country’s 228 local governments currently enforce setback distances, with existing requirements for solar projects running from 100 to 1,000 meters. The government says this variation has constrained the availability of suitable sites for renewable energy development.
Lee Kyung-soo, MCEE’s Director General of Renewable Energy Policy, said the amendment will increase the predictability of renewable energy projects while also considering public acceptance.
“We will continue to communicate with local governments to ensure the system is stably established on the ground and contributes to the expansion of renewable energy supply,” he added.
Further amendments to South Korea’s enforcement decree also establishes a new legal framework governing new energy and renewable energy sources.
Rather than encompassing such energy sources under once act, the framework is being separated to govern renewable energy under the Act on Promotion of Development, Use and Dissemination of Renewable Energy and hydrogen and other new-energy provisions governed under the Act on Promotion of Hydrogen Economy and Hydrogen Safety Management.
Last week, a groundbreaking ceremony took place for South Korea’s
largest single-site PV complex
to date. In July, the country announced its latest solar tender covering
1 GW of new solar capacity
South Korea’s cumulative solar capacity reached 30,346 MW by the end of 2025, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), a 3.6 GW increase on data reported at the end of 2024.

title: Around 14 GW of irregular distributed solar threatens grid security in Brazil, warns TÜV Rheinland - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Unauthorized distributed-generation expansions in Brazil could add up to 14 GW of unregistered capacity, complicating grid planning and operation, TÜV Rheinland warns. The expansion of PV systems up to 5 MW without proper design reviews or approvals also raises electrical safety risks and compliance concerns.
Alessandra Neris
12 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Image: Nikola Johnny Mirkovic / Unsplash
The undeclared expansion of distributed solar photovoltaic generation has evolved from a regulatory issue into a matter requiring greater attention in the planning and operation of Brazil’s electricity system, while also increasing technical risks at individual installations, according to Vinicius Gibrail, director of the Solar and Commercial Products Division at TÜV Rheinland in South America.
The issue is central to Public Consultation 009/2026 by the National Electric Energy Agency (Aneel), which proposes regulatory measures to address surplus energy and increase operational flexibility within distribution networks. Among the proposed measures is a crackdown on unauthorized changes to the original specifications of micro- and mini-distributed generation (MMGD) systems, which in Brazil include all PV installations not exceeding 5 MW in size.
The consultation is based on Technical Note No. 148/2025-STD/Aneel, which documents reports from distribution companies of unauthorized increases in MMGD capacity, as well as warnings from the National Electric System Operator (ONS) about the impact of distributed generation on the operation of the National Interconnected System (SIN).
According to ONS estimates cited in the regulatory process, unauthorized additional capacity could reach 14 GW. The figure represents distributed generation capacity that is not adequately reflected in official records.
“Failure to notify Aneel of expansions—whether by an individual or a company—keeps the additional capacity hidden. This is not only illegal but also imposes additional costs on other consumers, similar to traditional energy theft,” Gibrail said.
System impact
Undeclared generation can widen the gap between the capacity actually connected to the grid and the capacity recorded in databases used by distribution companies and the ONS.
“Since this energy is not registered, the ONS does not factor it into its projections and operational decisions,” Gibrail said.
Technical Note 148/2025-STD/Aneel links unauthorized system expansions to the management of surplus energy within distribution networks. However, this does not mean irregular generation is solely responsible for curtailment. Rather, the core issue is the increased uncertainty over the actual amount of generation available at a given time.
Safety risks
Beyond their impact on system planning and operation, expansions carried out without a design review can compromise the electrical safety of individual installations.
“Generation systems must adhere to the standards set by the Brazilian Association of Technical Standards (ABNT). Installations must comply with ABNT NBR 16690:2019—which establishes design requirements for photovoltaic array installations—and NBR 5410, which covers low-voltage electrical installations, to ensure safety and proper operation,” Gibrail said.
According to Gibrail, projects should also involve a qualified professional registered with the Regional Council of Engineering and Agronomy (CREA), with the corresponding Technical Responsibility Annotation (ART) issued.
He also emphasized the importance of using equipment that complies with applicable technical standards, including PV modules, inverters, and protection devices.
“Solar energy generation enables Brazil to maintain a clean energy matrix that fosters economic development. However, for this process to occur safely, projects must be properly regularized, technical certifications must be met, and certified equipment must be used,” Gibrail said.

title: Colombia: Earthquake affects power grid, but no damage reported at solar plants - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A magnitude-7.4 earthquake in Colombia disrupted electricity supplies, leaving up to 20% of demand unmet in some affected regions. No damage has been reported at utility-scale solar plants, with the main impacts concentrated on transmission and distribution infrastructure.
Luis Ini
12 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Americas
Utility-scale
Image: José Antonio Gallego Vazquez
The earthquake that struck Colombia on Monday had a magnitude of 7.4, with its epicenter in the municipality of San José del Palmar, in the department of Chocó, at a depth of 103 km, according to the Colombian Geological Service (SGC). The earthquake occurred at 7:34 a.m. and was the strongest recorded in the country so far this century. More than 200 deaths have been reported to date.
The SGC said the earthquake was felt in nearly 900 population centers, reaching a maximum reported intensity of 7, corresponding to severe damage. By midday Monday, 18 aftershocks with magnitudes ranging from 1.4 to 4.8 had been recorded. The agency attributed the earthquake to the subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate.
18% of demand initially unmet
In the electricity sector, grid operator XM reported that approximately 18% of national demand went unmet immediately after the earthquake. The disruptions were concentrated in the departments of Caldas, Caquetá, Cauca, Chocó, Huila, Nariño, Putumayo, Quindío, Risaralda, Tolima, and Valle del Cauca.
According to XM, the main impacts were not at power generation plants but on assets belonging to the Regional Transmission Systems (STR) and Local Distribution Systems (SDL). Following contingency and recovery operations, demand served by the National Interconnected System (SIN) had recovered to approximately 99% of pre-earthquake levels by the end of Monday.
However, recovery was not complete as of Tuesday. Available reports indicate that the Coffee Axis (Eje Cafetero) and Chocó still had approximately 20% unmet demand. In Valle del Cauca, the figure stood at around 18.5%, while in Cauca and Nariño it was approximately 5%.
No damage reported to solar generation assets
As of publication, there have been no public reports of physical damage to modules, trackers, inverters, or other equipment at utility-scale photovoltaic plants as a result of the earthquake. Available information indicates that the main impacts on the electricity sector have instead been concentrated on evacuation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure.
Celsia, a company with a significant photovoltaic presence in several affected regions, reported after the earthquake that some of its transmission and distribution assets, as well as certain substations, experienced outages or service interruptions. However, the company said its generation infrastructure and Nova Control Center were not affected and continued to operate normally and safely. Celsia did not provide a breakdown of this assessment by generation technology.
The information is particularly relevant to the photovoltaic sector because Celsia operates numerous solar plants in Valle del Cauca and Tolima, two departments where power supply disruptions were reported. Its facilities in Valle del Cauca include La Victoria 1 and 2, with 19.9 MW each; Palmira 1, with 19.9 MW; Buga, with 9.9 MW; Yumbo, with 9.8 MW; Tuluá, with 9.95 MW; La Paila, with 9.9 MW; and El Carmelo, with 9.8 MW.
In Tolima, Celsia’s portfolio includes Flandes and Dulima, with 19.9 MW each, as well as San Felipe, Lanceros, Yuma, and Espinal, each with approximately 9.9 MW. The company says it currently operates 25 solar farms with a combined installed photovoltaic capacity of more than 480 MW.
The impacts observed so far highlight the distinction between the physical integrity of generation assets and the availability of the electricity grid. A photovoltaic plant can sustain no structural damage yet still face temporary limitations in delivering electricity if substations, transmission lines, or distribution networks associated with its point of interconnection are taken out of service.

title: US eases transport rules for portable lithium batteries, raising limits and cutting regulation - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The shift to battery-powered tools and portable power stations in the trades has been hampered by hazardous materials regulations set before the battery revolution. A new US ruling better clears the way for the portable storage industry.
Tristan Rayner
12 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
United States
Image: Bluetti
The transition to battery power on the job site is seemingly inevitable, but in the US, hazardous material classifications were relatively strict for commercial-sized operations. For contractors actually hauling gear, the logistics themselves have been strangling adoption. When scaling up, portable power stations may have seen some unwittingly classified as hazardous materials transporters.
A long-awaited regulatory update from the
Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), part of the Department of Transport (DOT), is fixing a bottleneck with a 16-part rulemaking change.
The regulation update, known HM-268A through HM-268P, was published as the set of 16 changes earlier this month by PHMSA/DOT, with most changes taking effect on September 3, 2026.
While the rules modernize many types of freight regulations, the standout for the battery sector is the new
, which focuses on weight classifications for lithium-ion batteries.
A previous bottleneck was at the 200 kilograms or 440 pounds scale, which was the outdated limit the industry bumped up against. Previously, lithium batteries were treated under the general limitations for any Class 9 hazardous material under the Materials of Trade (MOT) exceptions. For a service technician or contractor, the limits were restrictive, and the total gross weight of all hazardous materials on a single motor vehicle could not exceed 200 kg (440 pounds), meaning it was shared with other hazardous materials that may accompany a worker on a truck, such as fuel or paint. The weight of the entire device, such as an electric lawnmower, may have also counted toward the aggregate limit if the battery was installed.
The Portable Rechargeable Battery Association (PRBA) petitioned for the change, a group including companies such as Apple, Amazon, and Toyota, covering all manner of devices and technology, small and large.
Unlocking trades and portable power
The new HM-268C rule carves out a much-needed exception, effectively treating mid-sized lithium batteries as tools of the trade rather than strictly regulated hazardous freight.
The update expands the vehicle aggregate limit specifically for lithium batteries, raising it to 500 kg (1,102 pounds), effectively meaning several portable power stations or commercial replacement batteries in a standard work truck can now be carried without triggering heavy freight regulations and documentation, or the need for drivers with Hazmat endorsements.
On an individual level, workers can transport spare batteries weighing up to 30 kg (66 pounds) each. And, in another win for practical applications, the weight of batteries that are already securely installed in equipment is exempted and no longer counts toward the per vehicle cap.
The rules relax packaging requirements as well, and if spare batteries are securely fastened in the vehicle to prevent movement and potential damage, outer packaging is no longer strictly necessary.
Catalyst amid new headwinds
For the broader battery industry, the implications extend beyond compliance. The Institute of Hazardous Materials Management (IHMM) notes the update will generate a projected $14.4 million in annualized savings for trades like construction, landscaping, and entertainment. But more importantly, it removes major psychological and administrative barriers to electrification, with the effective green light potentially driving many times more on that figure across positives from switching from fuels to electricity.
However, the US faces challenges from other directions. Last week,
blocked new foreign-made inverters that are used in batteries from certification
, effectively banning most non-domestic brands from presenting new products. Existing products already certified remain on the market. A large portion of the portable battery market, from leading brands like Anker Solix, Bluetti, EcoFlow, and Jackery, is manufactured in China and other foreign nations.

title: 93% of US nuclear reactor fuel foreign-sourced, core loads at 41M lbs
content: Commercial nuclear power plants in the United States loaded 40.9 million pounds of uranium into their reactor cores in 2025. This was a 15 percent drop from the 48.1 million pounds installed during 2024. “Uranium in fuel assemblies loaded into US civilian nuclear power reactors during 2025 contained 40.9 million pounds U3O8e, which is 15% less than the 48.1 million pounds loaded in 2024,” highlighted a report from the US Energy Information Administration.At the same time, power companies expanded their overall fuel reserves. Total commercial uranium stocks increased by 9 percent, reaching 170 million pounds by the end of 2025. These reserves contain material at various technical stages of the nuclear fuel cycle. They include raw uranium undergoing chemical conversion, material undergoing isotopic separation, and finished fuel rods ready for reactor cores. Reactor operators owned 118 million pounds of this total, which is a 3 percent increase over 2024 levels. “Uranium inventories owned by U.S. suppliers (converters, enrichers, fabricators, producers, brokers, and traders) totaled 51 million pounds U3O8e at the end of 2025, up 27% from 2024 year-end levels,” added the report.Over the next decade, American nuclear utilities will require a massive volume of fuel to maintain grid operations. Over the next 10 years, operators project a total baseline demand of 360 million pounds of uranium. Current long-term purchase agreements cover 174 million pounds of this requirement. The remaining 186 million pounds represent unfilled market demand that utilities must secure through new contracts.Preparing raw uranium for power generationPreparing raw uranium for power generation requires distinct chemical and technical processing steps. “In 2025, COOs delivered 32 million pounds U3O8e of natural uranium feed to U.S. and foreign enrichers,” remarked the report. Domestic enrichment plants processed 37 percent of this material. Foreign facilities handled the remaining 63 percent, which included major shipments of 5.5 million pounds to France and 2.4 million pounds to Russia.Isotopic enrichment is measured in separative work units. This metric measures the effort needed to separate fissile uranium-235 from non-fissile isotopes. US utilities purchased 13 million separative work units from four commercial sellers in 2025. “The average price paid by the COOs for the 13 million SWU was $108.70 per SWU in 2025, up 11% from the $97.66 per SWU paid in 2024,” noted the report.Foreign facilities provided 77 percent of these enrichment services. Russian enrichers supplied 26 percent of the total, followed by France at 18 percent, the United Kingdom at 14 percent, and the Netherlands at 8 percent. US enrichment facilities supplied the remaining 23 percent.Procurement volume declined but transaction costs increasedOverall uranium procurement declined in volume, but transaction costs increased. “The 2025 total of 46.9 million pounds U3O8e was 16% lower than the 2024 total of 55.9 million pounds U3O8e,” concluded the report.However, the weighted-average price rose 11 percent, moving from $52.71 per pound in 2024 to $58.46 per pound in 2025. Long-term contracts accounted for 87 percent of total deliveries at an average price of $55.91 per pound. Spot market purchases made up 13 percent of deliveries at a much higher average price of $76.01 per pound. Operators also signed 22 new purchase contracts during the year, securing 4 million pounds for 2025 delivery at an average cost of $70.46 per pound.Foreign mining operations supplied 93 percent of all uranium delivered to US reactors, while domestic production accounted for just 7 percent. Canadian facilities served as the leading supplier by providing 32 percent of all deliveries. Kazakhstan followed closely with 28 percent, while Australia supplied 15 percent. Uzbekistan provided 7 percent and Namibia supplied 4 percent. Specific delivery numbers for Russian-origin material were withheld by regulators to protect commercial confidentiality. Data from the Euratom Supply Agency shows that Canadian and Kazakh mining operations also remained the primary uranium suppliers for European power utilities throughout the same period.

title: JCB’s 1,600-hp hydrogen car hits 406 mph in world speed record attempt
content: JCB’s hydrogen-powered Hydromax streamliner has reached 406.320 mph (653.2 km/h) at Utah’s Bonneville Salt Flats, setting a provisional world land speed record for a hydrogen internal combustion vehicle. The run took place on August 11, with Wing Commander Andy Green OBE behind the wheel. The record still needs formal ratification by the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA).The 32-foot British-built car made two runs in opposite directions within one hour, following FIA requirements for a flying kilometer record. It recorded 400.623 mph on the first pass and 412.135 mph on the return. Those figures produced a two-way average of 406.320 mph.A new benchmark for hydrogen combustionHydromax’s result more than doubles the previous FIA-recognized hydrogen internal combustion record. That mark was 185.5 mph, set by BMW’s H2R in 2004.The attempt falls into FIA Category A, Group XIV, Class 7 World Flying Record Start Land Speed Record. Final certification is still pending, so the 406.320 mph figure remains provisional.The car also moved beyond several major hydrogen and diesel milestones. It surpassed JCB Dieselmax’s 350.092 mph diesel record from 2006, which Green also drove at Bonneville. JCB said Hydromax produces no CO₂ at the tailpipe. Its speed also exceeded the 303 mph record previously achieved by a hydrogen fuel cell vehicle.Two production-based engines deliver 1,600 hpJCB built Hydromax around two hydrogen-fueled internal combustion engines derived from its production “digger” engines. Together, they produce 1,600 horsepower. The engines are manufactured at JCB’s facility in Foston, Derbyshire, England.The company says the power units are fundamentally the same hydrogen combustion engines being developed for its construction equipment. The program forms part of JCB’s £100 million hydrogen development effort.The approach gives the streamliner a direct connection to technology intended for working machines. Rather than using fuel cells to convert hydrogen into electricity, Hydromax burns hydrogen inside modified combustion engines.Green returns to BonnevilleJCB Chairman Anthony Bamford said the attempt builds on the company’s Dieselmax achievement at Bonneville two decades ago.“Twenty years ago we came to Bonneville with JCB Dieselmax and showed what British engineering could do with diesel power. Today we have done it again—this time with engines powered by hydrogen,” Bamford said.Green, who holds the outright land speed record at 763.035 mph and is the only person to break the sound barrier on land, described the project as a privilege.“Bonneville is the spiritual home of the world land speed record, and JCB Hydromax has just written itself into that history,” he said, calling the streamliner “stable, strong and fast” while praising “a world-class team and superb technology.”Speed test set the stageHydromax had already shown its pace during a warmup appearance at the Southern California Timing Association’s Bonneville Speed Week. It recorded a 368.347 mph average in the Blown Gas Streamliner AA/BGS 500-plus cubic inch class, setting a new SCTA mark before the latest record attempt.

title: US nuclear fusion facility to solve tritium fuel crisis for reactors
content: Japanese company Kyoto Fusioneering is relocating its primary US office to East Tennessee. Working with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the firm plans to build a specialized testing facility called UNITY-3. The project receives funding from the US Department of Energy along with support from Tennessee’s Nuclear Energy Supply Chain Investment Fund. The initial agreement behind this project began in January 2026.The main technical goal of UNITY-3 is to solve a major fuel problem in fusion energy. “A fusion power plant runs on tritium, a hydrogen isotope that barely exists in nature, so the plant must breed its own fuel inside a lithium-bearing shell wrapped around the fusion reaction,” explained the company in a press release.UNITY-3 does this by placing a shell containing lithium around the fusion reaction. This shell, known as a breeding blanket, absorbs neutrons from the reaction to create fresh tritium.However, tritium breeding technology remains one of the least developed areas in nuclear engineering. Without working blanket systems, commercial fusion cannot function. UNITY-3 aims to test and de-risk these systems before full-scale power plants are built.Fits into broader US energy plansThe new facility is equipped with a particle accelerator that generates high-energy fusion neutrons across a broad volume. Researchers will place prototype blankets inside this neutron environment to measure how much tritium is produced. They will also track how neutrons move through the materials. These physical measurements will help engineers correct and improve the computer codes used to design future fusion plants. Currently, no other facility combines this exact source shape, component scale, and deep measurement capability.This testing approach fits directly into broader US energy plans. The Department of Energy recently released its Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap, which identifies blanket testing as an urgent technical gap. Beyond hardware testing, UNITY-3 will also produce high-fidelity scientific data. This data will be fed into the Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission, specifically helping to train AI models for the AI-Fusion Digital Convergence Platform. These digital tools are designed to simulate reactor performance and speed up engineering timelines.Third stage of overall testing strategyThe project forms the third stage of Kyoto Fusioneering’s overall testing strategy, known as the UNITY program. Rather than testing every component at once, the company isolates different physical processes across separate sites. The first facility, UNITY-1 in Kyoto, Japan, tests non-nuclear liquid-metal systems, focusing on heat transfer, liquid flow in magnetic fields, and power generation alongside Idaho National Laboratory. The second facility, UNITY-2 in Ontario, Canada, demonstrates a continuous tritium fuel processing loop in partnership with Canadian Nuclear Laboratories and Savannah River National Laboratory. “UNITY-3 adds the critical fusion-nuclear dimension — the neutronics, tritium production validation, and transmutation effects that can only be measured in a real fusion-neutron environment,” concluded the press release. UNITY-3 operates as an open facility that works regardless of a reactor’s specific plasma design. Several fusion companies, including General Atomics, Realta Fusion, OpenStar Technologies, Thea Energy, Xcimer Energy, and Type One Energy, have supported the project as a shared tool to test their designs.By settling in East Tennessee, Kyoto Fusioneering gains access to the regional nuclear workforce, local suppliers, and research staff at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. In return, the firm brings Japanese fusion hardware and manufacturing capabilities directly into the local industrial network.

title: World’s largest green hydrogen facility nears commissioning
content: Saudi Arabia has reached a major milestone in its ambition to become a global leader in clean energy as the construction now finished on the NEOM Green Hydrogen and Ammonia project, one of the most ambitious green-hydrogen developments ever undertaken.According to the project’s developer, ACWA Power, construction of the $8.4 billion facility has been completed and the complex has entered the commissioning phase. Commercial operations are targeted for 2027. Carbon-free hydrogenOnce operational, the facility will produce up to 600 tons per day of carbon-free hydrogen, converted into green ammonia for global export, providing a practical blueprint for green hydrogen at scale.Located at Oxagon in NEOM, northwestern Saudi Arabia, the project is being developed by a joint venture between ACWA Power, Air Products and NEOM. Once operational, it is expected to become the world’s largest green-hydrogen facility by electrolyzer capacity, representing a significant step forward for large-scale renewable hydrogen production. Large-scale solar and wind power generationThe project combines large-scale solar and wind generation with electrolyzers that will use renewable electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. The hydrogen will subsequently be converted into green ammonia for transportation and export to international markets.The facility has an electrolzer capacity of approximately 2.2 GW, supported by around 4 GW of dedicated renewable power generation from solar and wind. At full production, the plant is designed to produce as much as 600 tons of carbon-free hydrogen per day, which will be converted into up to 1.2 million tons of green ammonia annually. This scale is particularly significant because green hydrogen production remains relatively fragmented worldwide. The NEOM project is designed to demonstrate that renewable hydrogen and its derivatives can be produced commercially at industrial scale rather than only through smaller demonstration facilities.Construction marks the beginning of commissioningThe completion of construction marks the beginning of another critical stage: commissioning.NEOM Green Hydrogen Company said its renewable-energy assets, including the wind farm, solar farm and transmission infrastructure, had reached advanced stages of completion earlier this year. The company subsequently moved toward energization and commissioning of the hydrogen-production equipment. The transition from construction to commissioning is crucial because the project must now demonstrate that its interconnected renewable-energy, electrolysis, hydrogen-processing and ammonia-production systems can operate together reliably.ACWA Power CEO Samir Serhan revealed that the plan is for commercial operation to begin in 2027, indicating that the project has moved beyond the construction phase and into preparation for actual production. Hydrogen is difficult and expensive to transport over long distances in its pure form. Converting hydrogen into ammonia provides a more practical way of moving large quantities of renewable energy between continents.Green ammonia can also be used directly in industries such as fertiliser production and potentially as a low-carbon fuel for shipping and other applications.For the NEOM project, ammonia is therefore more than simply an end product. It is a means of connecting Saudi Arabia’s abundant renewable-energy resources with international markets.The project secured a long-term off-take arrangement for its green ammonia, helping provide the commercial foundation required to finance the development. The original financial close in 2023 involved $8.4 billion of total investment and $6.1 billion in non-recourse financing from 23 banks and financial institutions. The project also reflects a broader shift in Saudi Arabia’s energy strategy. For decades, the Kingdom has been synonymous with oil and gas. Through projects such as NEOM, however, Saudi Arabia is seeking to use its strong solar and wind resources to establish itself as a major producer and exporter of renewable energy and clean fuels.The country’s geography provides a potentially important advantage. Vast areas of land, high solar irradiation and suitable wind resources can support large renewable-energy installations, while the Kingdom’s existing industrial and export infrastructure could help connect new clean-energy products with global markets.The NEOM project is consequently being positioned not simply as a hydrogen plant, but as part of Saudi Arabia’s broader economic diversification and industrial strategy.The project is also expected to contribute to reductions in greenhouse-gas emissions by replacing hydrogen and ammonia produced using fossil fuels.Earlier project assessments estimated that the facility could avoid as much as 5 million tons of CO₂ emissions annually once fully operational. The actual climate benefit, however, will ultimately depend on how efficiently the facility operates, the performance of its renewable-energy assets and the carbon intensity of the production and supply chain. These factors will become clearer once the plant begins commercial operations.

title: Intel silicon quantum chip points to hidden atomic disorder that disrupts qubits
content: Scientists in the US have found a hidden atomic disorder inside silicon quantum devices that could help answer the long-standing question of why some qubits fail or perform inconsistently.The project was carried out by a team at Argonne National Laboratory (ANL). The researchers studied an industrially manufactured 12-qubit-class silicon quantum dot processor from Intel. For the study, they used highly sensitive measurements to map variations in the material at the nanoscale. Their analysis traced the long-standing qubit problem to random changes at the atomic level.The findings could lead to the development of more reliable silicon qubits and larger quantum computers. Silicon spin qubits are promising because they can use existing semiconductor manufacturing methods. “This study revealed that disorder on the atomic scale in the quantum well is the main source of variability of valley splitting,” ANL said. Tracing qubit failuresUnlike conventional computer bits, which represent information as either 0 or 1, silicon spin qubits rely on the spin of individual electrons. An electron’s spin can point up or down in a magnetic field, somewhat like a tiny compass needle.To create these qubits, scientists trap a single electron inside an extremely thin layer of silicon known as a quantum well. Electrons in silicon also have another quantum property known as a valley state. The energy difference between these states is called valley splitting.The Chicago quantum computing testbed at Argonne National Laboratory (ANL).Credit: Argonne National Laboratory (ANL)Valley splitting competes with the electron spin states used to perform quantum computations. Once the splitting becomes too small, the electrons can leak into unwanted valley states. This can lead to errors and reduce the fidelity of the qubit.That said, valley splitting can vary greatly between devices. Even though the team suspected that material defects and inconsistencies played a role, the underlying cause of these variations remained unclear. To investigate the issue the research team used the Chicago Quantum Computing Testbed, which is operated by the Q-NEXT National Quantum Information Science Research Center. The facility is the first full-stack, solid-state qubit testbed at a US National Laboratory.Testing silicon qubitsThe scientists relied on electrical spectroscopy to measure valley splitting while moving the position of a quantum dot along the silicon quantum well. This made it possible to create a nanoscale map showing how valley splitting changed from one location to another.They then evaluated how these variations changed across different distances and found that random atomic changes in the alloyed quantum well were the main cause of valley splitting variability.Knowing where the variability originates could help semiconductor manufacturers to focus on improving the materials and fabrication processes for silicon quantum device production. The collaboration linked Intel’s semiconductor manufacturing with ANL’s quantum expertise.According to Jonathan Marcks, PhD, a scientist at ANL, the work could speed up research by removing one of the field’s biggest hurdles. “It can be difficult to build even a few quantum dot qubits,” he said in a press statement. “But with Intel, the prospect of making a ton of qubits on a practical device using quantum dots suddenly seems a lot more realistic.”Reducing the atomic variations could help manufacturers produce silicon qubits with more consistent valley splitting and higher fidelity. This could make it easier to scale quantum processors to much larger numbers of qubits. The research was funded by the US Department of Energy’s Office of Science through the Q-NEXT center.The study has been published in the journal Nature Communications.

title: 24-hour warning for ballistic missile tests: US, allies raise demand
content: Just a month after China shocked every nation with a long-range ballistic missile test in the Pacific, the U.S. and other countries have called for a warning before any such planned launch.The U.S. Department of State issued the ‘Joint Statement on Notifications of Ballistic Missile Launches’, which has also been signed by 40 other countries. The countries include Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Turkiye, Great Britain, among others.The call for issuing advance notifications includes prior notice for the launch of intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs), and space launch vehicles (SLVs) to affected states.The joint statement mentions that the recent missile testing in the Pacific region “did not follow the standard practices adopted by most states to notify and deconflict ICBM, SLBM, and SLV launches.” However, China is not named in the joint statement, but all references to the missile test point towards Beijing’s recent launch.Conducting nuclear-capable ballistic missile tests with advance noticeThe joint statement calls on all countries, particularly the ones which have nuclear weapons in their arsenal, to issue advance warning for ballistic missile launches. It goes on to add that conducting “nuclear-capable ballistic missile tests without sufficient advance notice and detail is dangerous and disrupts the peace and security of relevant nations in proximity to these tests.”Moreover, the joint statement warns that such tests increase the risk of miscalculation and undermine global stability and security.
